summary: Provides background information for the Internet Accounting Architecture, a way to measure network usage. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains why counting how much network people use could matter.

questions: where should accounting meters be placed
subtitle: The reasoning behind a 1991 plan to measure network usage with meters, collectors and flows.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew and more organizations ran parts of it, there were few tools to measure who used how much of the network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adopts the OSI accounting model of meters, collectors and applications, and argues for meters that count packet flows in or near routers at administrative boundaries.
tldr.outcome: It is background for an architecture and meter service that were still under construction, limited to usage reporting rather than billing or enforcement.

today: RFC 1272 is an Informational memo from November 1991, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states that it does not specify an Internet standard, and that the architecture and meter service documents were still under construction when it was written.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1272 is the first of a three document set: this background document, an Internet Accounting Architecture and an Internet Accounting Meter Service. The latter two were still under construction. The focus is on meter services and usage reporting, meaning the semantics for measuring utilization, a syntax, and a data reporting protocol.

The aim is a practical standard for early experimentation. The short-term solution is meant to merge with OSI and Autonomous Network Research Group (ANRG) efforts and be superseded by them in the long term. It deliberately does not cover applications such as enforcing policy, recommend billing approaches, or settle who pays for retransmitted packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors are only trying to work out how to count network use. They are not deciding who should pay.

sections.title: Why Report Usage, and What It Costs
sections.content:
The memo gives three motivations: helping subscribers understand and change their behavior, letting providers measure policy compliance, and supporting cost allocation or recovery, up to billing. The costs are reporting and collection overhead, post-processing overhead, and security overhead. The balance is set by the granularity of the data collected, which should be the minimum needed for a given policy.

The memo is cautious. Flat-fee access charges can be preferable for financial, technical and social reasons, while usage-sensitive charges may be required by regulation or wanted by low-volume users. Before meters are used for billing and enforcement, the memo says they should first be used to understand user behavior, quantify network improvements and measure compliance with policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting costs effort, so you should only count as finely as you really need to.

sections.title: The Accounting Model
sections.content:
The memo adopts the OSI accounting framework (ISO 7498-4), which has three entities: the meter, which measures and aggregates; the collector, which keeps meter data intact and secure in short-term storage and transit; and the application, which processes, formats and stores the data. This work specifies meters and collectors.

The model assumes a network administrator who owns an administrative domain with defined boundaries. He is interested in traffic inside and crossing those boundaries, but only accounts to the level of directly adjacent domains. Charges then percolate back recursively to the end user. Because adjacent-system usage cannot be derived from end-system accounting, accounting needs information not present in IP headers, which carry only end-system addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper counts, one helper keeps the counts safe, and one helper reads the numbers. Each neighbor only keeps track of the neighbor next door.

sections.title: Meters, Placement and Granularity
sections.content:
A meter examines a stream of packets and records aggregate counts for flows between communicating entities. Full accuracy needs every packet examined, but statistical sampling may do when accuracy can be relaxed. Meters are most needed at administrative boundaries, and the memo finds routers the most generally convenient place, for three reasons: lower cost, the ability to act on quotas, and the ability to see adjacent systems.

Four metering types are listed: network monitors, line monitors, router-integral meters and router spiders. Granularity runs along four dimensions: entity (from port through network to host), attribute, values such as packet and byte counts, and reporting interval. Each entity, attribute and interval combination is a separate meter that uses memory.
sections.plainLanguage: The best place to count visitors is at the doors, not in every room. Counting in finer detail needs more notebooks.

sections.title: Collection and Open Issues
sections.content:
Collection is to be mapped onto an SNMP framework where possible. The main concerns are data confidentiality, data integrity, and local and remote collection control. Reliable delivery can use acknowledgment and retransmission, redundant reporting to multiple collectors, or backup storage at the meter. Polling lets the collector pace data but adds overhead, while meter traps are needed anyway so a full meter can shed data.

The memo does not decide whether to count packets on entry to or exit from a router, and requires that both be possible. Its worked examples run from a single LAN to a national backbone. Left for the future are application standards, quotas, session accounting, application-level accounting, and an IP option to identify the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Counts are private, so they must be delivered safely and not lost. Whether to count visitors going in or going out is left for later.

viz.caption: OSI ACCOUNTING ENTITIES USED BY RFC 1272

items.title: Meter
items.text: Performs measurements and aggregates the results.

items.title: Collector
items.text: Responsible for the integrity and security of meter data in short-term storage and transit.

items.title: Application
items.text: Processes, formats and stores meter data; implicitly manages meters.
